# Summary: 2005 Manifesto - Britain Forward

## Economic Policy
The manifesto emphasizes maintaining economic stability through low inflation targets, fiscal prudence, and sustained investment in public services. Key commitments include keeping income tax rates unchanged, maintaining the minimum wage with planned increases, and achieving full employment across all regions. The goal is an 80% employment rate, with particular focus on helping those on incapacity benefits back to work through rehabilitation programs.

Economic growth would be supported through investment in skills, science, infrastructure, and reduced regulation. A ten-year science strategy aims to increase research and development spending from 1.9% to 2.5% of national income by 2014. Transport investment exceeding £180 billion through 2015 is pledged, including potential road pricing systems to address congestion.

## Education
The education agenda focuses on personalized learning, with targets for 85% of pupils achieving high literacy and numeracy standards by age 11. Every secondary school would become an independent specialist school, with 200 new Academies established in disadvantaged communities by 2010. The Building Schools for the Future program would modernize school facilities over 15 years.

Vocational education would be strengthened through specialized diplomas and apprenticeships designed with employers. Educational Maintenance Allowances of £30 weekly would help lower-income students stay in education past 16. Higher education funding reforms would cap fees at £3,000 annually, with increased grants and bursaries for poorer students.

## Healthcare
NHS investment would triple by 2008 compared to 1997 levels. The maximum wait from referral to treatment would be 18 weeks by 2008, with no hidden waits. Patient choice would expand, allowing selection of any hospital for treatment. New community hospitals would provide diagnostics, day surgery, and outpatient services closer to communities.

Public health measures include restricting advertising of unhealthy foods to children, improving school meals with 50-60p minimum spent on ingredients, and workplace smoking restrictions (with licensed premises exempted from full bans). Death rates from heart disease and cancer would be targeted for significant reductions.

## Crime and Security
Neighborhood policing teams would be established in every community, with Community Support Officer numbers rising to 24,000. Anti-social behavior powers would be extended, including anonymous evidence provisions and alcohol disorder zones. Compulsory drug testing at arrest for property and drug offenders would be introduced, with mandatory treatment assessments.

Identity cards with biometric data would be introduced voluntarily as passports are renewed. A points-based immigration system would prioritize skilled workers, with mandatory English tests for permanent settlement. Electronic border systems would track visitors entering or leaving the country by the end of the period.

## Families and Social Policy
Child poverty targets include halving it by 2010-11. Paid maternity leave would increase to nine months by 2007, with the goal of one year by Parliament's end. Universal childcare for ages 3-14 would be developed, with 3,500 Sure Start Children's Centres established.

Home ownership would expand by another two million through various schemes including shared ownership, equity loans, and increased stamp duty thresholds. Social housing supply would increase 50% by 2008.

## International Affairs
The manifesto supports the European Constitutional Treaty, to be put to referendum. The independent nuclear deterrent would be retained. International development aid would follow a timetable to reach 0.7% of national income by 2013. Climate change leadership would continue, with commitment to 60% carbon dioxide reduction by 2050.

## Governance
House of Lords reform would continue with removal of remaining hereditary peers. Local government would receive greater freedoms, reduced inspection burdens, and three-year funding stability. Wales would receive enhanced legislative powers for its Assembly. Council tax reform would be considered following the Lyons Review.
